author: SA Editor Mike Taylor, CFA
title: Holiday Shopping During The Apocalypse
text:
Dear ESSENTIAL subscribers,
Hi! I'm Seeking Alpha managing editor Mike Taylor. Welcome to ESSENTIAL Weekly, a subscriber-exclusive look at Seeking Alpha's top news and analysis. I'll guide you through this week's market themes, highlight some analysis you might have missed, and preview coming attractions for SA subscribers.
Don't be bashful: We need to hear from you so we can make ESSENTIAL the best investment research tool available anywhere. Let me know directly what the Seeking Alpha team can do -- your feedback is key to our success.
Now let's get to the good stuff.
Holiday Season During The Retail Apocalypse I'm not a monster, so I bought Christmas presents for my family this past December. I did what I could online early in the month, but honestly was super exhausted from hosting Thanksgiving and work-related travel, so a lot of my gift-buying was not online, but in person.
In other words, like a true Peter Lynch type, I went to the mall. I bought my brother a Giannis Antetokounmpo jersey (Go Bucks!) at Macy's ( M ). I bought my other brother a cookbook from Barnes & Noble ( BKS ). I bought sister a board game from a store in a Brookfield Properties Group ( BPY ). I batted 1.000 on Christmas day. It was beautiful.
And it should have been beautiful for all these companies. More than half my shopping was brick and mortar, baby!
Turns out America may have zigged where I zagged. On Thursday, The Wall Street Journal's top story (paywall) focused on brick-and-mortar retailers' continuing struggles even while the economy hummed along through a nice holiday season. Seeking Alpha's news team documented the related sector-wide slump .
The author community is trying to make sense of it all. Seeking Alpha author Dividend Diplomats also put on a Peter Lynch hat , but headed over to Kohl's ( KSS ), and found a lot to like there. The online shopping experience was positive (Instant-Pot: purchased), and the customer service was good. Meanwhile, the stock itself meets a lot of relevant screening criteria, and the company seems to be handling its debt load responsibly.
Elsewhere, Raul Shah disagrees with the market's treatment of Target following Q3 earnings. Josh Arnold is neutral on Williams-Sonoma , but likes RH . Shock Exchange wrote a bearish note on Bed Bath & Beyond ahead of Wednesday's quarterly report, and so far the market has strongly disagreed, as shares are up strongly since then. Amid the confusion, we'll have to stay tuned for more updates on how the holiday season went.
I was at the Kase Learning short-selling conference in December. There, David Berman argued that the true picture of U.S. retailers includes Amazon ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ). I believe it is time for us to update our broad approach to the space, and it "feels" like a lot of the seismic shifts have already taken place. It'll be fun to see whether investors go back to the old "retail is dead" refrain or reach for a new way to see the space.
No Trade Deal? No Big Deal You're not supposed to get in a trade war.
That's not exactly a business school proverb, but for a long time it was conventional wisdom. I came of age in the 1990s, read The Economist in college, and spent most of my formative years swimming around in the assumption that slow evaporation of international trade barriers was inevitable, and by coincidence mostly good. Trade wars, or anything else that impedes free flow of goods and capital across borders, are bad. So the argument went, anyway. (For analysis steeped in this perspective, I recommend Kristina Hooper's piece on the trade war. I also recommend Chinese Internet Weekly , which is exclusive for ESSENTIAL subscribers.)
So I was surprised and a little disappointed to read that there may not be that much left to worry about. In " The Trade War Is Over, We Won ," Mercator International Opportunity Fund ( MOPPX ) portfolio manager Herve van Caloen says China's president Xi Jinping repeated a mistake made by many of President Trump's opponents -- underestimating the U.S. president's tenacity.
[Xi] thought that if he waited a bit, the Trump administration would cave in. [...] As it turns out, this President is different. He fires those members of his cabinet who try to reverse his policies. Instead of letting his policies revert back to the status, president Trump insists on real results.
van Caloen concludes, alluding to China's weak economy, that Xi will have to cave, since economic stability is key to preserving social order there. A resolution, he says, "will be a big relief for China, for the U.S. stock market and for the world economy." It's a compelling argument, and while it provoked strong reactions among readers (900+ comments), I think investors would do well to focus on the economic arguments and decide for themselves what the implications are for their portfolios.
Not all authors agree with van Caloen. John Engle took the other side : The trade war is not over, and China may very well emerge victorious. Citing the many political battles Trump has to fight domestically, Engle sees Xi as in a much stronger spot politically:
Now effectively president-for-life, Xi naturally has a very different set of priorities from those of Trump. The American president can at best hope to win a second and final term in 2020, but either way he will be out of the picture ere long. Given Trump’s deeply negative approval rating, it is not unreasonable for Xi and his inner circle to conclude that Trump can be waited out.
Engle, like van Caloen, sees the possibility of a China retreat as a positive for markets, but more uncertainty if the U.S. eventually backs down.
I generally have trouble incorporating macro trends into my own portfolio decisions. The takeaway from the debate, for me, is more that you can have a directional view if you want, but anything can happen: no one has any excuse to be surprised by the direction U.S. stocks take in the short term -- up or down.

The House Of Cards That Is Chinese Real Estate Let's Not Kid Ourselves... The Market Will Remain Under Pressure Dividend Investors, Mind Your Leverage How leveraged are you?
Seeking Alpha focuses primarily on liquid publicly traded securities -- mostly stocks and funds. A lot of our articles are zoomed in on this important part of any investor's total portfolio. But this focus can paint an incomplete picture. The funds that go into an investor's brokerage account come from somewhere. Some investors choose to secure these funds by using margin debt.
Following a wild December for stocks, Dividend Sensei is paying down his margin debt . The benefit of debt is that it magnifies returns. The drawback is that it also magnifies downside, and it can leave portfolios vulnerable when volatility increases. As Long Term Capital Management found out, leverage can blow up even a strong investing strategy if the unexpected happens, even for a short time. As Dividend Sensei says:
With margin, you absolutely have to worry about other people. If our leaders (specifically President Trump or Fed Chairman Jerome Powell) mess up badly enough, the economy and the stock market could be sent spiraling into a crash that could make even the smartest long-term strategy fail catastrophically.
I have a mortgage, and am fortunate that my household has no other debt, but I appreciate the insight here. I'm not much of an economic forecaster. Like a lot of investors, I like to watch the yield curve for a recession signal, and I've enjoyed reading the tea leaves along with everyone else. But the yield curve isn't a perfect indicator, and it's less useful for stock returns than for signaling recessions.
But we're not just investors, we're also people. I often tell Daniel that my objective as an investor is not to lose my job the next time there's a recession. He laughs at that, but I'm not really joking. After all, the guy who wrote " Ten Years Ago, Almost Everyone in Media Got Fired " was once my boss.
I think Ray Dalio is a smart person. I don't think I want to work for him , but I am mindful of his comments about managing your human capital and financial capital through a downturn .
If you have a bearish view of the markets, you might want to think about some of the basics. I've never used margin, but I know I'm not about to start this week.
Now some stock picking.
Investing In The Dating Sector I am not positive that investors appreciate the extent to which dating has changed in the past decade (the timing, incidentally, of my graceful exit from the dating scene). But dating has changed a lot, in ways that I don't think are always perceptible even to today's singles, let alone people like me who are now married and have left that world behind.
So is it possible that, even at lofty valuations, The Meet Group ( MEET ) and Match Group ( MTCH ) are attractive buys?
After reading Detroit Bear's concise and compelling long thesis on MTCH in late December, Daniel and I published a Behind The Idea podcast on Match Group on Tuesday. As we were talking, I started to come around to the idea that Match crown jewel Tinder's roughly 20% share of the North America dating market could easily reach 30%, its subscriber conversion rate could 1.5x to 10%-12%, and just by these estimates alone, revenue could more than double. That's without touching possible faster international growth or synergies with Match's other brands (Match, PlentyOfFish, OKCuped) or its majority stake in Hinge.
While all these relationship-tech companies may be exciting, it's important not to lump all of them together too tightly. This week, Eight Diamonds Advisors published an Editor's Pick on The Meet Group ( MEET ). He argues that MEET is playing for a wider, more casual variety of human experience than Tinder's freemium hookups.
Match’s main growth driver at present is Tinder frequently referred to as a ‘hookup’ not ‘dating’ app. For MEET, Live Video is the emerging value driver.
Eight Diamonds' broad point is that after a bout of acquisitions, MEET is in execution phase, it's generating free cash flow to help pay down debt, and it's trading at an EV/sales multiple less than half that of Match's. Our editors liked this article because it identified a strong mispricing based on a headwind, offered a balanced discussion, and let readers know to look out for signs of slowing revenue growth. It didn't help that MEET doesn't get a ton of mainstream coverage.
(For a very strong counterpoint, investors should check out The Friendly Bear's 2016 article on some of MeetMe's business vulnerabilities.)
A key question for each business model is -- how much will dating play out via video (advantage: MEET ) vs. in person (advantage: MTCH ).
